summary: LunaWolf is a free browser game that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost for 30 days. Players balance oxygen, power, radiation shielding and food while solar flares, dust storms, equipment failures and the long lunar night test their plans. After every action and event, the game explains why it happened, so students learn the real engineering trade-offs behind a mission instead of just reading about them. It runs on any phone or computer with no install, which makes it easy to use in a classroom.
details:
What it does: The player is the commander of an outpost on the Moon or Mars. Each day the player gets two actions, such as installing solar panels, running the oxygen generator, piling regolith on the habitat for radiation shielding, tending the greenhouse, or mining materials. Then the day ends, the crew uses oxygen and food, the shield wears down, and random events may strike. If any of the four life-support bars reaches zero, the mission fails. Surviving 30 days wins.

Why it works for learning: Every choice costs something. Oxygen and food production use power, shielding uses power and materials, and solar panels stop working at night or in dust storms. Students experience that fixing one system stresses another, which is the core challenge in the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer statement. Each action and event shows a short "Why" note that connects the game to real space science.

Two destinations: On the Moon, a long night removes solar power, so the player must stock up beforehand. On Mars, sunlight is weaker and a dust storm season cuts solar output, and help from Earth is far away.

Planning and feedback: A mission control forecast tells the player when the lunar night or dust storm season is coming, so students learn to plan instead of just react. There are three difficulty levels (Cadet, Commander, Mission Director). When a mission ends, a debrief chart shows how all four resources changed over time, with a lesson that explains what went wrong or right. Best scores are saved in the browser.

Testing: The game logic is separate from the screen code and is covered by 17 automated tests. We also simulated thousands of games with two bots to check the balance. A planning bot wins most Commander games (about 86% on the Moon, 81% on Mars), while a random bot almost never wins, so student choices matter. The Mission Director level is much harder (about 55% Moon, 38% Mars for the planning bot).

Benefits: Free, works offline once loaded, mobile friendly, no account needed, and the numbers and lessons are easy for teachers to edit in one file.

Tools used: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), Node.js for automated tests, VS Code, GitHub Pages for hosting.

Future work: More events, a crew health bar, a classroom score board, and more languages.
